_about: Player Tributes: the fifth AI-authored lane (owner-approved 2026-11-14, "both yes"). A long-form feature per player on his whole career, keyed POS:Name, written only by a tribute.set upload mutation; every figure cited in stats[] with its source and checked like the Season Story (scripts/story_check.py check_tribute). Never hand-edit.

QB:Sherman Brandson.reason: Correction: Michael Wilson's number is retired by the Vikings (2026-11-17-wilson-father-son)
QB:Sherman Brandson.trigger: Owner moved Michael Wilson's retired number
QB:Sherman Brandson.deck: Wherever Dorren Skura went, he was under center: Baltimore, Tampa Bay, New York. He waited out the lean years in Minnesota until the coach came back, threw for more yards and touchdowns than anyone the league has seen, and in Y95 finally handed over the crown.

chapters.headline: Baltimore, Where the Long Ball Became a Habit
body: Sherman Brandson's first rings came in Baltimore, on a Ravens club Dorren Skura had already turned into a machine. Y46 set the tone: 16-0-1 in the regular season and a 32-24 win over the Seahawks in Super Bowl CV. In week 3 of that season he found D. Haley for a 77-yard touchdown against the Browns, still the longest passing play on Skura's record board.

The Ravens went 17-0 in Y48 and beat the Rams 16-9, then 16-1 in Y49 and beat the Eagles 36-28. Y50 was the one that got away: another 17-0 regular season, a 58-yard touchdown run by Denzel Hayes on a Brandson handoff against the Dolphins that is still the longest on the board, and a 36-32 loss to the Saints in Super Bowl CIX. He left Baltimore with 3 rings, and Baltimore has since retired his number.

chapters.headline: Tampa Bay, and a Title Won Against His Old Club
body: When Skura moved to Tampa Bay for Y51, Brandson moved too, and the Buccaneers did not lose a step. They went 16-1 and routed the Jaguars 40-13 in Super Bowl CX. A year later they went 16-1 again and met the Ravens in Super Bowl CXI, Brandson against the club where he had won his first rings. Tampa Bay won 32-25.

Y53 was the cruelest season of his prime. The Buccaneers went 17-0, the only perfect regular season of his three in Tampa Bay, and still went out in the championship round. The Titans won that title instead, 36-31 over the Eagles, and Brandson's run of titles stopped at two in Tampa Bay.

chapters.headline: New York, and the Season Nobody Has Come Close To
body: Skura took the Giants job for Y54 and Brandson was under center again. The Giants went 16-1 and beat the Jets 36-28 in Super Bowl CXIII. Then came Y55, the season that still defines him. He threw 94 touchdown passes, the most in a season on Skura's record board, and nothing in the league's tracked seasons since has come within 22 of it; Bones Crawford's 72 in Y89 is the nearest. Nine of them came in a single game against the Chiefs, the club the Giants beat 68-21 in Super Bowl CXIV.

He played three seasons in New York and is remembered first as a Giant. Y56 made it three titles in three years: a 14-2-1 season and a 38-37 escape against the Bills in Super Bowl CXV. The club has retired his number and keeps him in its Ring of Honor beside Jackson Wardell Kline.

chapters.headline: Minnesota: The Long Wait, Two More Rings, and an Unfinished Chase
body: Brandson spent Y57 through Y60 in Minnesota without a ring while Skura won three straight titles in Miami. Then, for Y61, the coach came to the Vikings, and the old partnership picked up as if it had never stopped. The Vikings went 12-5 and beat the Ravens 40-14 in Super Bowl CXX, another title won against Baltimore. They went 14-3 in Y62 and beat the Jaguars 40-24, 40 points in both Super Bowls.

Y62 was also his last season, and it ended too early. Injury cut it short while he was on pace for the best passing season on Skura's record board, Dennis Baylon's 7,452 yards from Y33, a mark that still stands. The same season his receiver God Johnson, then Mason Earl III, caught for 4,247 yards, still the best receiving season on the board. Y62 is also where the board dates both of Brandson's career marks: 91,463 passing yards and 1,150 touchdown passes. He retired a Viking with 10 rings. Minnesota, New York and Baltimore all retired his number.

stats.label: Career TD passes (club record)
stats.source: records.json Most TD passes, career mark

chapters.headline: Michael Wilson, the Quarterback Who Inherited Minnesota
body: Michael Wilson, "Air Wilson", never shared a huddle with Brandson. He spent Y60 through Y62 in Baltimore without a ring while Brandson was finishing in Minnesota, then took over the Vikings for Y63, the season after injury ended Brandson's career. The dynasty did not miss a beat: Wilson won 5 rings there in six seasons, throwing to God Johnson, who set the career receiving record on Skura's board in Y67. Side by side, the careers are not close. Wilson completed 72 percent of his passes, Brandson 84.7. Wilson threw for 58,992 yards and 690 touchdowns in 214 games; Brandson for 91,463 and 1,150 in 315. Wilson won 6 MVPs, Brandson 8. Both now hang in Minnesota's Ring of Honor.

chapters.headline: The Most Valuable Card in the League, Until Y95
body: Brandson has not thrown a pass in the market's lifetime, and his card has still climbed. It was valued at 36,912 after Y80 and 40,388 after Y94, rated 99 with an A+ grade the whole way, the most valuable card in the league at every season's end. Each new season rescales Career Legacy, and a frozen line like his only looks better against it. Y95 was the first time another card finished above it: Ryland Maxwell's, at 44,400 to his 40,657.

chapters.headline: The Numbers
body: In 315 games: 91,463 passing yards, 1,150 touchdown passes at 3.65 a game, 84.7 percent of his passes completed and only 50 sacks taken. 10 rings, 8 MVPs and 4 Super Bowl MVPs. No Offensive Player of the Year award ever came, the one gap on a shelf full of MVPs.

chapters.headline: Y95, the Year the Crown Changed Hands
body: For as long as the market has measured it, Brandson held the top Career Legacy in the league. After Y94 he led Ryland Maxwell by 381. Maxwell added 912 in Y95 and finished it at 14,019, 479 ahead of Brandson's 13,540. The passing records are another matter. His 91,463 yards lead Wayne Wilson, "The Mailman", by 1,013, his 1,150 touchdown passes lead by 237, and the Hall of Fame ballot scored his case at 100, a perfect mark only Rondale Ikarras and God Johnson share.

QB:Ty Lock.reason: The Y96 tribute pick (tributePlan: retired, retirement recorded in Y96)
QB:Ty Lock.deck: Two rings and two MVP awards with Dorren Skura's Jets, then a trade across town and thirteen seasons as the Giants' steady hand: a quarterback who outlasted almost everyone and never once beat his old coach's Eagles.

chapters.headline: Two Rings and Two MVPs Before New York Let Him Go
body: Ty Lock came into the league with Dorren Skura's Jets in Y78, at 22, and it did not take long. By the end of Y80 he owned a ring, won when a 15-2 club edged the Seahawks 28-26 in Super Bowl CXXXIX, and the league's Most Valuable Player award. His card was still priced at 20, a starter's price, not a star's.

Y81 was the loudest season of his life: 4,411 passing yards and 51 touchdown passes in 18 games and a second MVP, for a 14-2-1 club that still watched someone else play for the title. Y82 went one better. Lock threw for 4,909 yards and 61 touchdowns, the Jets beat the Eagles 46-8 in Super Bowl CXLI, and he was its MVP.

He was a gambler then. He threw 92 interceptions in his first 93 games, and nobody in New York minded, because the touchdowns kept coming: 239 of them in five seasons, with 22,189 yards and an A+ grade on his card. Then the winter came and the coach left town.

chapters.headline: Across Town in the Winter of the Four-Way Trades
body: The winter after Y82 rearranged the league. Skura left the Jets for Atlanta, and a run of three- and four-team trades moved starters all over the map. Lock ended up with the Giants. The Jets replaced him with Dan Stout, a 79-rated veteran from the Ravens, and the Giants' own quarterback, Drake Wise, went through Atlanta to Baltimore without playing a game for the Falcons.

By the market's reading that winter, New York got the bargain. Lock's card was worth 63, Wise's 869, though Lock had the rings, the MVPs and the better grade, and Wise had no rings at all. It took years for the prices to catch up. Neither quarterback won anything after the deal: Wise played 105 more games and retired a Raven, and Lock played 237 more in a Giants uniform without another ring.

stats.label: Lock's card value at the trade
Wise's card value at the trade

chapters.headline: The Gambler Who Stopped Throwing Interceptions
body: The quarterback New York got was not the one the Jets had. In Y83, his first Giants season, Lock threw 33 touchdown passes, barely half the 61 of the year before, and his grade slid from A+ to A− even as his rating climbed to 73. The volume was gone. So, almost entirely, were the mistakes.

From Y84 through Y88 he threw 11 interceptions in 90 games, a single one in all of Y88, when he threw 38 touchdowns. Over his years as a Giant he threw 45 interceptions in 237 games, after 92 in 93 with the Jets. He became the safest quarterback a club could ask for and one of the most durable: never fewer than 17 games in a season.

The ratings kept climbing with him. He reached 89 in Y90 and an A grade, and the Giants, 9-8 in Y88, went 11-5-1 in Y91 and 11-6 in each of the next two seasons. What they never did was get past Philadelphia.

stats.label: Fewest games in a Giants season (Y86, Y88, Y94)

chapters.headline: Seventeen Tries Against His Old Coach, Seventeen Losses
body: When Skura took over the Eagles in Y88, the coach who had won Lock his two rings moved into his division. They met twice a season, and the Giants lost every time: 17 meetings through Y95, 17 Philadelphia wins, 572 points to 374.

Some were routs, none worse than 48-9 in Y90. Many were not. The Giants lost 22-21 in Y89, 38-37 in Y92, 24-23 in Y93 and 32-31 in Y95. The cruelest came in the Y93 conference final, a game from the Super Bowl, when the Eagles won 38-28 to end an 11-6 Giants season.
Lock outlasted almost everyone else in the league. He never found a way past the coach who had made him.

chapters.headline: A Card That Climbed for Thirteen Years Without a Ring
body: The market came around to Lock slowly and then all at once. His card was worth 63 when he left the Jets and 108 after his first Giants season. It reached 1,110 after Y88 and 2,928 after Y91, and in Y93, a season his touchdown passes fell from 32 to 26, it still rose 30%. After Y94 it passed Wise's for the first time, 5,090 to 5,074, years after Wise had played his last game. It closed at 5,810.

chapters.headline: Lock and Wise: Two MVPs Each, Only One With Rings
body: The quarterback who left the Giants as Lock arrived makes the cleanest comparison. Wise threw for 64,703 yards and 641 touchdowns in 347 games; Lock for 68,237 and 627 in 330. Each won 2 MVP awards. Wise was the safer passer by far, 62 interceptions to Lock's 137, and he never won a ring. Lock won 2, both before the trade. The final Career Legacy, 7,550 to 7,473, gives Lock the edge by a whisker.

chapters.headline: The Final Numbers
body: His career, complete: 68,237 passing yards and 627 touchdown passes in 330 games, 105 more touchdowns on the ground, 2 rings, 2 MVP awards and a Super Bowl MVP.

chapters.headline: Thirty-Nine, Rated Higher Than Ever, and Done
body: Y95 was his last season, at 39, and he played it like a man in no hurry to leave: 3,488 yards, 31 touchdown passes and 4 interceptions for a 10-6-1 Giants club, with his rating at a career-high 94. The Eagles still beat New York twice, the first time 32-31. Then the retirement was recorded, and he did not play again. The Hall of Fame has not voted him in. The record says he is the rare quarterback who won his rings early, outlasted almost everyone, and never needed them to be worth watching.

RB:Ryland Maxwell.deck: He came out of New York as the smallest piece of a trade and became the back every other back is measured against: rings in three cities, the career rushing record and, at last, the Gauntlet.

chapters.headline: A Ring in New York Before Anyone Knew His Name
body: Ryland Maxwell's first ring came in Y80, when Dorren Skura's Jets went 15-2 and beat the Seahawks 28-26 in Super Bowl CXXXIX. Maxwell was part of it and nowhere near the center of it. His card closed that season rated 62 with a C grade, and the market valued it at 7, the kind of price reserved for depth.

Y81 brought 1,284 rushing yards and no title. Y82 brought both: 1,430 yards, 17 rushing touchdowns and a second ring after a 46-8 rout of the Eagles in Super Bowl CXLI, a club he would one day call home. Through three seasons in New York he had 3,514 rushing yards in 56 games and an Offensive Rookie of the Year award on the shelf. Useful. Not yet a reason to build a franchise around him.

chapters.headline: One Star Out, Three In, and the Smallest Piece Was the Prize
body: When Skura left New York for Atlanta after Y82, the deal that went with him looked lopsided, just not the way it turned out. Malakai Sawyer went back to the Jets as an 89-rated back with a B grade, 203 games and 13,041 career rushing yards, his card priced at 1,755. Coming the other way were Maxwell, rated 65 and valued at 12, Chance Woodrum, a 74-rated defensive back valued at 70, and Kane Van Oxley, "The Ox", an S-grade receiver valued at 1,515.

Was it a risk? By the numbers that winter, Sawyer's card was worth more than a hundred times Maxwell's, and the best asset Atlanta received never played for it: in an offseason of three- and four-team trades across the league, Van Oxley was moved on to the Bears before a single Falcons game. The bet came down to Maxwell and Woodrum. Sawyer played 96 more games and won no more rings. Woodrum won 5 more. Maxwell won 11.

chapters.headline: Five Straight Titles, and the Role Player Disappeared
body: Atlanta won Super Bowl CXLII in Y83, beating the Jets and Sawyer 40-25, and did not stop winning them until Y87. Maxwell was Offensive Player of the Year in that first season, with 1,919 rushing yards and 25 touchdowns on the ground, and Super Bowl MVP the next.

The ratings followed the rings. He was rated 75 by the end of Y84, an A grade at 87 by Y86 and an S at 96 by Y87. Y85 was the season the league took notice: 2,617 rushing yards, 39 rushing touchdowns, still the season mark on Skura's record board, and a 237-yard game against the Bills, still the best rushing game on it. Another Offensive Player of the Year award came with it. By the end of the run he had 7 rings and 15,141 career rushing yards.

stats.label: Rushing TDs, Y85 (club record)
stats.source: records.json Most rushing TDs, season mark

chapters.headline: Left Behind in Atlanta
body: Then Skura moved on to Philadelphia for Y88, and Maxwell stayed. The Eagles won Super Bowl CXLVII that season and CXLVIII the next, the coach's titles now arriving without the back who had carried his last five. In Atlanta, Maxwell kept running: 1,403 yards in Y88, 1,172 in Y89 and 1,223 in Y90, without a single catch in the last two of those seasons. No rings came.

The market did not seem to mind. In Y88, with no title to show for it, his card passed Sawyer's for the first time, 7,837 to 7,820, and by the end of Y90 he was rated 99. The best back in the league was waiting in the wrong city.

chapters.headline: From 7 to 49,485, a Season Late Every Time
body: The card told the story a season late every time. It was worth 7 at the end of Y80 and 12 on the day of the trade. It reached 112 after Y84, with two Falcons titles already won, and 1,520 after Y86. It first passed Sawyer's in Y88, at 7,837, and more than doubled in Y92 alone, from 12,722 to 29,409, the season he ran for 2,839 yards. After Y94 it stood at 39,532, and it stood at 49,485 after Y96, with another season still to come.

chapters.headline: The Reunion, the Record and the Gauntlet
body: In Y91 coach and back were together again in Philadelphia, and the titles came back with them: four seasons, four rings, starting with a 38-23 win over the Raiders in Super Bowl CL. Y92 brought 2,839 rushing yards, the best season on Skura's record board, and in Y93 Maxwell passed Lane McCoy's 24,507 career rushing yards to take the league record. Along the way the Eagles won 49 straight games, a run that only ended in Dallas in Y94.

Y94 was a season nobody had seen before. Maxwell caught 53 touchdown passes, the most in a season on Skura's board, and was named Most Valuable Player for the first time. It was the one major award he had never won. With it he became the first player to win every one of them: a ring, the MVP, Offensive Player of the Year, Super Bowl MVP and Offensive Rookie of the Year. Ryland Maxwell ran the Gauntlet.

chapters.headline: Ikarras, the Measuring Stick
body: Every great back gets measured against Rondale Ikarras, "The Prodigal Son", the Ravens legend of the Hall of Fame's inaugural class. The comparison has gone Maxwell's way. Ikarras ran for 23,178 yards in 303 games, 76.5 a game; Maxwell has 32,108 in 323, 99.4 a game. Ikarras won 9 rings to Maxwell's 13 and 4 Offensive Player of the Year awards, one more than Maxwell, but 5 Super Bowl MVPs to his 7. He never won the MVP. Maxwell won it once, and it completed the set.

stats.label: Ikarras Offensive Player of the Year awards

chapters.headline: The Numbers Through Y96
body: His career through Y96: 32,108 rushing yards, 421 rushing touchdowns and 125 more through the air in 323 games, with 13 rings and a Career Legacy of 14,903, the highest of any player in the league, and Y97 still to play.

chapters.headline: Two More Rings, First All Time, and One More Year at 35
body: There was no argument left to settle, and he played on anyway. In Y95 he ran for 2,141 yards and won a 12th ring, playing 18 of the Eagles' 20 games after injury cost him 2, and passed Sherman Brandson for first in Career Legacy, 14,019 to 13,540. Y96, at 34, was better still: 2,574 yards and 25 rushing touchdowns in 21 games, a 13th ring after a 40-26 win over the Bengals, and a 7th Super Bowl MVP, with the career rushing record now at 32,108 yards.

Then, instead of leaving on top, he re-signed with Dorren Skura. He opens Y97 at 35, still an Eagle. The Hall of Fame watch already scores him at 100, the maximum, and the Hall can wait one more year.

WR:God Johnson.reason: The Y97 tribute pick (tributePlan: queue, no one cleared the bar; the queue's highest Career Legacy)
WR:God Johnson.deck: Every season he played, he played for Dorren Skura, first in Miami and then in Minnesota. He arrived as Mason Earl III, changed his name along the way, and left as God Johnson, holder of the league's receiving records and a ring for almost every year he played.

chapters.headline: Miami, Where Mason Earl III Learned What Winning Felt Like
body: He came into the league in Y58 at 22, under another name. Mason Earl III joined a Dolphins club Dorren Skura had just taken to a title, and he joined it at full speed. Miami went 15-2 and beat the Cowboys 40-33 in Super Bowl CXVII, and the rookie receiver had a ring in his first season.
Y59 was a demolition. The Dolphins went 16-1 and buried the Lions 46-9 in Super Bowl CXVIII, and he already stood first among the key players of Miami's run, ahead of Marlowe Hunter and Rod Kuechly.

Y60 is the one Miami still turns over. Another 16-1 season, another trip to the Super Bowl, and this time the Cowboys got even, 28-24 in Super Bowl CXIX. He left Florida with 2 rings in three seasons. When Skura took the Vikings job for Y61, the young receiver went north with him, and the league would not see the end of that partnership for nine more years.

chapters.headline: Two Seasons With Brandson, and a Receiving Year Nobody Has Touched
body: Minnesota already had Sherman Brandson under center and Jackson Wardell Kline at the other receiver spot. Add Skura and the young man from Miami, and the Vikings went 12-5 in Y61 and beat the Ravens 40-14 in Super Bowl CXX.

Y62 is the season his name is attached to forever, though the name on the record board is the old one. Mason Earl III caught for 4,247 yards, the best receiving season on Skura's board. Nothing in the seasons the league has tracked since has come close: the next best is Kaulani Rahman's 2,635 for the Eagles in Y89, a gap of 1,612 yards. The Vikings went 14-3 and beat the Jaguars 40-24 in Super Bowl CXXI.

It was also the last season of the partnership. Injury ended Brandson's career that year, with the passing records he still holds already on the board. The quarterback who made the receiver was gone. The receiver was about to prove he did not need him.

chapters.headline: A New Name, a New Quarterback, and the Same Result Every February
body: Michael Wilson took over in Y63, and the Vikings did not blink. They went 16-1 and beat the Jets 40-31 in Super Bowl CXXII, then went 16-1 again and survived the Chargers 40-39 in Super Bowl CXXIII. Wilson won 5 rings in Minnesota, and the man he threw to was there for every one.

Somewhere after Y62, Mason Earl III became God Johnson. The name drew smiles. The production did not. By Y67 the club's record board carried his name twice, for career receiving yards and career touchdown catches, and those totals passed Ian Finney's to lead the whole league.

Y65 was the lone blemish of the decade: a 16-1 season that ended short of the Super Bowl. Minnesota answered with back-to-back 17-0 seasons, beating the Chiefs 38-25 and the Steelers 40-24, and re-signed him in Y66 along the way. Kline was beside him the whole run and collected 6 Offensive Player of the Year awards to Johnson's 3. Johnson took 5 Super Bowl MVP awards. When the lights were brightest, the ball found him.

chapters.headline: Johnson and Finney: The Record and the Man Who Held It First
body: Before Johnson, the receiving records belonged to Ian Finney, "The Infinity Man", who won his rings in Washington and Tampa Bay decades earlier. Finney caught 1,902 passes for 32,980 yards and 292 touchdowns in 250 games. Johnson caught 2,081 for 36,005 and 378 in 234, which is 3,025 more yards and 86 more touchdowns in 16 fewer games. Finney won 5 Offensive Player of the Year awards to Johnson's 3, but Johnson has the rings, 10 to 9, and the Super Bowl MVPs, 5 to 3.

chapters.headline: A Retired Receiver's Card That Never Stopped Climbing
body: He had been retired for a decade when the market first priced him, in Y79, at 31,983, second only to Brandson. He has not caught a pass since, and his card has risen 20% anyway, to 38,525 after Y97, because every new season rescales Career Legacy and a finished line like his only looks better against it. His Career Legacy went from 11,531 to 12,840. The one thing the market could not hold off was Ryland Maxwell: after Y94 the running back's 13,107 passed Johnson's 12,655, and Johnson has ranked third behind Maxwell and Brandson since.

stats.label: Card value at the first reading, Y79

chapters.headline: The Numbers
body: In 234 games: 2,081 catches, 36,005 receiving yards at 17.3 a catch and 378 touchdowns, one on every 5.5 receptions. He fumbled 3 times in his career. 10 rings, 5 Super Bowl MVPs, 3 Offensive Player of the Year awards and an MVP.

chapters.headline: Y69: One More Ring, Then the Hall Waited for Him
body: His last season came at 33, and it ended the way most of his seasons did. The Vikings went 14-3 and routed the Chiefs 48-18 in Super Bowl CXXVIII, his eighth title in Minnesota and his tenth in all. He retired a Viking, and Skura left for the Titans the next season. When the Hall of Fame opened its doors, he was in the inaugural class, his case scored at 100, the highest mark the ballot gives, and ranked first among receivers. Minnesota keeps him in its Ring of Honor.
